Original Guilt
oh-RIJ-ih-nul GILT
noun phrase
From Latin originalis (of origin, first) + Old English gylt (offense, crime, sin). Original guilt is the technical Reformed theological term distinguishing the forensic dimension of inherited sin from the moral dimension: it names the real legal liability that all descendants of Adam bear before God on account of Adam’s first transgression, as distinct from the inherited corruption of nature that is the other consequence of the fall.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Original guilt is the forensic component of original sin: the imputed legal liability of Adam’s first sin reckoned to all his natural descendants. Romans 5:12–19 is the definitive text. Paul teaches that through one man’s disobedience, the many were made (katestathêsan) sinners—not merely that all eventually commit sin and thereby become sinners, but that they stand in the condition of sinners by virtue of Adam’s transgression, before any act of their own (Rom. 5:19). This is the Augustinian and Reformed doctrine of the imputation of Adam’s sin: just as Christ’s righteousness is reckoned to the believer by imputation (2 Cor. 5:21), so Adam’s guilt is reckoned to all whom he federally represents. Paul grounds this in the parallel between Adam and Christ (Rom. 5:18): “as through one transgression there resulted condemnation to all men, even so through one act of righteousness there resulted justification of life to all men.” The structure is representational and legal in both directions. The doctrine of original guilt is distinct from but inseparable from the doctrine of original corruption: Adam’s first sin produced both a change in judicial standing (guilt) and a change in moral nature (corruption, total depravity). Every human being comes into the world both guilty before God’s bar and polluted in nature—both realities demanding the double cure that only Christ provides: justification removes the guilt; sanctification heals the corruption. The 1689 Baptist Confession (6.2–6.3) and Westminster Confession (6.3) both affirm this federal imputation.

Webster 1828 Definition

Guilt: the state of having committed an offense; criminality; the liability of a person to penalty for crime or for an offense against law or divine requirement; in theology, the guilt of Adam imputed to all his posterity.

expand to see more

GUILT, noun. Criminality; that state of a moral agent which results from his actual commission of a crime or offense, knowing it to be a crime, or violation of law; the neglect of a known duty.

2. (Theology) Original guilt: the liability of all mankind to punishment for the sin of Adam, in whose loins they were present when he transgressed; the federal guilt imputed to all descendants of the first man.

3. Distinguished from original corruption (or depravity): guilt refers to the legal standing before God's law; corruption refers to the moral condition of the soul.

GUILT'Y, adjective. (Theology) Applied to the whole race of Adam: obnoxious to punishment for his first offense; legally responsible for the violation of God's command in Eden.

Webster's grounding of guilt in legal standing before the law reflects the Reformed consensus that the primary consequence of original sin is not merely moral pollution but forensic condemnation requiring forensic justification.

Key Scripture

Romans 5:12 — "Therefore, just as through one man sin entered into the world — and death through sin, and so death spread to all men, because all sinned —"

Romans 5:19 — "For as through the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners — even so through the obedience of the One, the many will be made righteous."

1 Corinthians 15:22 — "For as in Adam all die — so also in Christ all will be made alive."

Psalm 51:5 — "Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin my mother conceived me."

Modern Corruption

Pelagianism denies original guilt entirely, making Adam’s sin merely an example of a pattern humans independently replicate; modern therapeutic Christianity and progressive evangelicalism evade the forensic weight of original guilt by reducing sin to patterns of harm or systemic dysfunction.

expand to see more

Pelagianism—condemned at the Council of Carthage (418 AD) and by every subsequent orthodox Christian confession—holds that Adam’s sin affected only himself, that human beings are born in the same moral condition as Adam before the fall, and that sin is entirely a matter of imitation and individual choice. On this view, there is no original guilt—only a succession of self-caused guilts. Scripture’s teaching in Romans 5 demolishes this: Paul explicitly teaches that death spread to all not merely because all sin individually but because of the one man’s transgression (Rom. 5:15, 17). Pelagianism makes Paul’s parallel between Adam and Christ incoherent: if Adam’s sin is not federally imputed, neither can Christ’s righteousness be federally imputed—and if imputed righteousness falls, justification falls.

Modern therapeutic Christianity sidesteps original guilt not by denying it philosophically but by never preaching it pastorally. Replacing the forensic language of guilt and condemnation with the therapeutic language of brokenness, dysfunction, and unhealthy patterns, contemporary preaching offers “healing” rather than justification—leaving congregants without the one cure that actually addresses their primary need before God: the declaration of righteousness in Christ that cancels the condemnation that entered through one man. The full weight of original guilt is not a pastoral liability; it is what makes the gospel of free justification genuinely good news.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin originalis (of origin) and culpa (fault, blame) combine to name the foundational liability: not a guilt contracted by personal act but received at the point of origin from the first man.

expand to see more

Latin originalis — of origin, first; pointing to the guilt that attaches to man from his origin in Adam rather than from his own later acts

Latin culpa — fault, blame; root of “culpability”—the legal responsibility for wrong that original guilt identifies as incumbent on all Adam's descendants

Hebrew ʿavon — iniquity, guilt, punishment; captures the double sense of moral wrong and its legal consequences that original guilt embodies

Greek katakrima — condemnation, penal sentence; Rom. 5:16's term for what came through Adam's one transgression—the verdict of guilty that fell on all his race

Latin imputatio — reckoning, crediting to one's account; the forensic mechanism by which Adam's guilt is assigned to his posterity and Christ's righteousness is assigned to believers

Usage

"The doctrine of original guilt is the necessary presupposition of the doctrine of justification: if all men do not stand genuinely guilty before God apart from Christ, then justification has no real forensic content—it becomes merely a change of attitude rather than a change of legal standing."

"David's confession in Psalm 51:5 (‘in sin did my mother conceive me’) is the OT’s most personal expression of original guilt: David traces his sinful nature not merely to personal choice but to conception—to the point of origin."

"The Reformed distinction between original guilt (forensic) and original corruption (moral) clarifies why both justification and sanctification are necessary: justification addresses the guilt; the Spirit's work of regeneration and progressive sanctification addresses the corruption."
